parts.title: The Case Study
parts.text: The school nurse challenged Naomi, Cesar, and Bao with a case study: a town where an **outbreak** of illness had suddenly spread through several neighborhoods. Their job was to act like disease detectives. Cesar began by explaining that every infection starts with a **pathogen**, a germ such as a virus or a bacterium. Bao added that the key question was **transmission**, meaning how the germ passes from one person to another, whether through air, food, or touch.

parts.title: Following the Clues
parts.text: The records showed a long **incubation** period of several days between catching the germ and feeling sick. That made the puzzle harder, because some residents were **asymptomatic**; they carried the germ without feeling ill, so they spread it without knowing. Naomi circled a note about poor **sanitation**, since the town's drinking water ran beside a leaking sewer. The nurse praised her: clean water and safe waste removal protect entire communities.

parts.title: How Communities Respond
parts.text: Next, the detectives studied the solutions. Clinics began to **sterilize** their instruments with heat, destroying every germ. Health workers set up stations to **inoculate** residents with a **vaccine**, which trains the body to recognize the germ. Bao explained that the body then builds an **antibody**, a protein that locks onto the germ and helps destroy it. Once enough people had **immunity**, the illness struggled to find new hosts. Had it crossed many countries, it would have been called a **pandemic**, but quick action kept this case local.

parts.title: Calm, Clear Facts
parts.text: When the case was solved, the three friends agreed that health depends on cooperation: clean water, careful science, and neighbors looking out for one another. Cesar said he now saw handwashing differently. Naomi planned to ask the nurse about starting a health club. Bao wrote on the board, "Calm, clear facts beat panic every time."

definitions.meaning1: A medicine, often given by injection, that prepares the body to fight a particular disease. Example: Children receive a vaccine that protects them from measles.
definitions.studentChallenge: The nurse explained that a single ___ can protect a child from a serious illness.

definitions.meaning1: The body's ability to resist a particular disease or infection. Example: After recovering from chickenpox, most people develop immunity.
definitions.meaning2: Protection from a legal duty or punishment. Example: Foreign diplomats have immunity from many local laws.
definitions.studentChallenge: Getting a vaccine helps your body build ___ without making you sick.

definitions.meaning1: A sudden rise in the number of cases of a disease in one place. Example: The outbreak was traced to a contaminated well.
definitions.meaning2: The sudden start of something unpleasant, such as a war or fire. Example: Nobody expected the outbreak of fighting along the border.
definitions.studentChallenge: Health officials rushed to the town to stop the ___ of the stomach illness.

definitions.meaning1: Conditions and systems, such as clean water and waste removal, that protect public health. Example: Better sanitation, including covered sewers, reduced illness in the city.
definitions.studentChallenge: Clean drinking water and safe sewers are the basics of good public ___.

definitions.meaning1: An outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world. Example: The pandemic changed how schools around the world operated.
definitions.studentChallenge: Because the illness spread across continents, health leaders called it a ___.

definitions.meaning1: To protect a person from a disease by giving them a vaccine. Example: Nurses worked all day to inoculate the students before flu season.
definitions.studentChallenge: Clinics hope to ___ every child in the village before winter.

definitions.meaning1: Infected with a disease but showing no signs of being sick. Example: An asymptomatic traveler can still pass the germ to others.
definitions.studentChallenge: Some people with the virus are ___, so they never realize they are infected.

definitions.meaning1: The period between catching a germ and showing signs of illness. Example: The flu has a short incubation period of one to four days.
definitions.meaning2: The process of keeping eggs warm until they hatch. Example: The incubation of the chicks takes about three weeks.
definitions.studentChallenge: Doctors track the ___ period, the days between catching the germ and feeling sick.

definitions.meaning1: To destroy all germs on an object or surface, usually with heat or chemicals. Example: Dentists sterilize their tools between patients.
definitions.studentChallenge: Boil the bottles for five minutes to ___ them before use.

definitions.meaning1: A protein made by the body that attaches to a germ and helps destroy it. Example: A blood test showed that her body had made an antibody for the virus.
definitions.studentChallenge: After the shot, the body makes an ___ that recognizes the germ.

definitions.meaning1: A germ, such as a virus or bacterium, that causes disease. Example: Soap helps wash away each pathogen that lands on your skin.
definitions.studentChallenge: Scientists identified the ___ responsible for the illness: a tiny bacterium.

definitions.meaning1: The passing of a disease or signal from one place or person to another. Example: Wearing a mask can slow the transmission of respiratory germs.
definitions.meaning2: The part of a vehicle that carries engine power to the wheels. Example: The mechanic replaced the car's transmission after the gears began to slip.
definitions.studentChallenge: Handwashing is one of the easiest ways to reduce the ___ of germs.

secretPassage.instructions: Read the passage below. Fill in each blank with the correct vocabulary word from the word bank.
secretPassage.passage:
Cesar's science fair poster began with a question: how does one tiny germ become a crisis? He explained that every illness starts with a _(1)_, such as a virus or bacterium. Its _(2)_, the way it passes from person to person, may be through the air, shared food, or touch. After the germ enters the body, a quiet _(3)_ period of several days may pass before anyone feels sick, and some people stay _(4)_ the entire time, never showing a single symptom.

When cases climb quickly in one town, health officials call the event a local _(5)_. If the illness crosses borders and sweeps across the world, it becomes a worldwide _(6)_. Cesar then described defenses. Good _(7)_, including clean water and safe waste disposal, keeps germs from spreading. Hospitals _(8)_ their instruments with high heat. Each _(9)_ prepares the body without making a person sick, and clinics work hard to _(10)_ every child. Afterward, the body builds a protective _(11)_ that recognizes the germ. When enough people are protected, the community enjoys shared _(12)_, and the illness runs out of places to spread.
